tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in messages from the system in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

---
name: vh-adlc-spec
description: Author or review a vh-adlc feature document, the single document that is both a feature's spec and its plan. Use only when the owner invokes /vh-adlc-spec or explicitly asks to specify, revise or review a feature with the vh-adlc loop; it is not the entry point for planning in general. Generic vh-adlc requests use lifecycle intake.
---

# vh-adlc-spec

## Saved owner summary

- When the resolved template includes `### Owner summary` inside Context, write that subsection for
  the owner before the background detail. Use its guidance rather than creating a second template.
  On a normative revision, refresh it against the changed scope; before acceptance, reconcile its
  decisions and proof wording with the current document. Keep planned checks distinct from observed
  results. Summary-only corrections do not create acceptance or change the normative baseline.
- Keep the conversation summary below even when the document already contains its saved summary.
  Untouched historical documents need no summary backfill; preserve returned review records exactly.

## Generic intake

For generic vh-adlc requests without an operation name, follow `references/lifecycle.md`; then continue here.

The plugin directory is two levels above this skill's own directory. Every path below that starts
with `references/` or `scripts/`, and `knowledge.md`, is in that directory.

Two modes: author (`/vh-adlc-spec <issue, goal or document>`) and review (`/vh-adlc-spec review <path>`).
Follow `references/loop.md` for every step it describes, `references/authority.md` for what you may do
without asking, and `references/review-protocol.md` for the review mode.

## Loop routes

This operation's loop role and route come from `.vh-adlc/loop.yaml` through
`bun scripts/loop/cli.ts route` (`references/loop-settings.md`); without the file, every role keeps the
host default. Before acting, read every file `bun scripts/loop/cli.ts context` lists: the repository's instruction
files and its project procedure, whose local rules apply alongside this procedure. A spec review also passes the declared lenses to the reviewer. A reviewer role's `command` route runs through `bun scripts/loop/cli.ts review` in place
of the host dispatch described below, as `references/review-protocol.md` (Routes) describes: a `ready`
outcome is stored like a host reviewer's records, and a `pending` outcome leaves the review pending. A
`host` route that names a model dispatches with it as a requested model.

## Issue labels

An issue this operation creates under acceptance or request gets one type label and no state label;
the feature document carries its state (`references/issues.md`). Run `bun scripts/labels/cli.ts file
--repo <checkout> --operation spec --type <type label>` with `--title`, `--body-file` and a new
`--output` file. It uses the repository's mapped label names. Show the owner the labels with the
title and body, then create the issue with `--preview <that file> --approved-digest <digest>`. When it
reports missing labels, create nothing and give its next step.

## Start

1. Get the binary and run `vh-adlc knowledge` with `conventions/feature-documents.md`,
   `guides/feature-document-template.md`, `conventions/documentation.md`, `conventions/delivery.md` and
   `guides/humanize-prose.md`. Report the one-line result. Read those pages from the cache before writing.
2. Run `vh-adlc find` with the issue number or the slug. If a document exists, extend it; never create a
   second document or a second issue for the same feature.
3. If the document has a `branch` field, work only on that branch in its owning worktree, and apply the
   handoff rule in `references/authority.md` before the first write. Otherwise work on the default branch
   in a worktree that holds it, without disturbing anyone's changes.

## Author mode

- Write from the template page at the resolved revision, into the feature root `vh-adlc knowledge`
  reported. A new document starts at the first status the standard gives; `find` returning nothing is what
  allows creating it.
- Ground every claim in a citation you gathered in this run: a `file:line`, a command and its output, or a
  source you read and list. Measure rather than remember.
- Write criteria as end states, each with a Test Plan row naming a real check.
- Where the design changes state, runs concurrently, or crosses a process or network boundary, state in
  Design what happens under concurrent requests, partial failure, retry or replay, and upgrade or rollback
  from the previous version. Put any of those choices you cannot settle into Open Questions.
- When you change a rule, limit or default, search the document for every other place that states it and
  change them all in the same commit.
- Put every judgement call into Open Questions in the standard's decision shape, and put each to the owner
  with the host's question tool. Never answer one yourself. Fold the owner's answers into the document. When
  the resolved convention states the nit rule, nits from a review pass are not Open Questions; review
  mode handles them under that rule.
- Creating an issue needs explicit authority.
- Run `vh-adlc lint` and fix what it reports before committing.

## Review mode

1. Commit the document first; a review targets an exact commit. Call it X. When `vh-adlc fresh` shows the
   spec review stale from drift alone (covered changes on the default branch, an unchanged baseline),
   first bring that work in. With a `branch` field, run `git merge origin/<default branch>` on the feature
   branch in its owning worktree; without one, run `git merge --ff-only origin/<default branch>` on the
   default branch. Git keeps unrelated uncommitted work through either. Let Git decide whether it can: if
   it refuses, report its message and stop, never stash or discard anything to get past it. If the merge
   changes the normative baseline, revise instead, as below. X is then the resulting commit.
2. Dispatch `vh-adlc-reviewer` as `references/review-protocol.md` describes, with the document, X, kind
   `spec`, the docs revision, the binary path and the plugin pin. If dispatch is impossible, write the handoff and leave
   the review pending.
3. Apply the model eligibility rules in `references/review-protocol.md` before storing anything.
   A requested model must match; an unrequested default may report `MODEL: unknown`,
   recorded as `unknown` with model identity explicitly not attested. Never infer its ID from the main
   session. If the protocol leaves the review pending, store nothing. Otherwise store the records
   after the header under the next `### R-<n>`, with a Review Log row at X naming the reported model,
   before changing anything. Then run `vh-adlc review check` against the same text.
4. Apply the pass's findings as one revision. First list the behaviors the design touches and every
   test, scenario and fixture the criteria and Test Plan name. Walk each finding, and every change it
   implies, through all of them, and re-read each named test or scenario before changing what it checks.
   Turn judgement findings into Open Questions for the owner first, without changing the baseline; when
   the nit rule below applies, nits are the exception. Once the owner has answered, apply every factual finding to be applied and every answer in
   one commit. Where a finding can be met by removing a mechanism or by adding one with the same
   behavior, remove it; where they behave differently, the choice is an Open Question recommending
   removal. Where a finding traces to a change the previous revision made, revisit that change instead of
   patching on top of it. List the behaviors and checks you walked in the report. A blocking pass is
   cleared only by a new independent pass at the new commit.

   The nit rule applies when the resolved `conventions/feature-documents.md` states it: its Review log
   section says that a baseline nit alone never triggers a revision. A page that only
   lists `nit` as a record value does not state it. When it applies, follow it in that same commit: fix
   every nit of the pass, factual or judgement and in any section, only when the pass's blocking or
   should-fix findings change the normative baseline, and never a free-text widening nit. Raise no nit as an Open Question. List every nit you did not apply, from every pass this run
   handled, with its review and finding IDs and one line, in your report and the owner-facing summary,
   not in the document. When the resolved page does not state it, apply a factual nit like any other factual
   finding and turn a judgement nit into an Open Question, as before the rule, and say in the report that
   the nit rule needs the plugin's own pin from `knowledge.md`.
5. When a clean review at X exists and Open Questions is empty, present the owner-facing summary below,
   then ask the owner to accept. On acceptance in session, append the acceptance row at X, run
   `vh-adlc gate planned`, and on a pass move the status and commit with the gate's line.

## Owner-facing summary

Whenever you finish spec work, summarize the current spec in the conversation. Before each acceptance
or renewed acceptance request, give the owner enough information to decide without reading the document
end to end or reopening earlier progress updates. Scale the summary to the feature; use plain language
and a few short paragraphs or bullets covering:

- The problem, intended outcome and proposed user-visible behavior.
- What is included, what stays unchanged or local, and what is excluded.
- Significant defaults, side effects, permissions and trade-offs.
- Migration, compatibility and rollback when relevant.
- The validation plan, current review result, and remaining blockers, limitations or deferred tests.
- Exactly what acceptance authorizes and which later actions still need separate approval.

For a revised spec, explain what changed since the last accepted version. Distinguish planned checks
from executed checks and spec review from implementation verification. Link the full document for
details; a link, review verdict or list of criterion IDs does not replace the summary. The document
remains the canonical scope and the existing acceptance and status gates still apply.

## Revising a planned or in-progress document

Before changing anything in the normative baseline the standard defines, run `vh-adlc gate draft` and
commit the move to draft on its own, on the feature branch when one is set. Then revise, review and accept
again as above. On a normative revision, reset criterion ticks and remove live evidence and residual lines;
their history stays in Git. Keep checked tasks and add new task IDs for changed requirements.

## Committing and pushing

Edit every prose section, commit message and report with `guides/humanize-prose.md` at the resolved
revision before writing it, and name the page and revision in the report. While the document has no
`branch` field, commit it (with first-run onboarding files) on the default branch and push those
documentation-only commits there, as the delivery convention at the revision describes for such
deliveries. A rejected push is a partial result: keep the commit and ask whether to open a PR instead.

## Report

What changed, the knowledge line, every `vh-adlc` result you acted on (quote its JSON `result` and `line`),
what was verified, what is left, including any review that is pending, and the page and revision used to
edit the prose.

   second document or a second issue for the same feature.

   handoff rule in `references/authority.md` before the first write. Otherwise work on the default branch

  reported. A new document starts at the first status the standard gives; `find` returning nothing is what
  allows creating it.
- Ground every claim in a citation you gathered in this run: a `file:line`, a command and its output, or a
  source you read and list. Measure rather than remember.
- Write criteria as end states, each with a Test Plan row naming a real check.
- Where the design changes state, runs concurrently, or crosses a process or network boundary, state in

  from the previous version. Put any of those choices you cannot settle into Open Questions.
- When you change a rule, limit or default, search the document for every other place that states it and
  change them all in the same commit.

  with the host's question tool. Never answer one yourself. Fold the owner's answers into the document. When

end to end or reopening earlier progress updates. Scale the summary to the feature; use plain language
and a few short paragraphs or bullets covering:

- What is included, what stays unchanged or local, and what is excluded.
- Significant defaults, side effects, permissions and trade-offs.
- Migration, compatibility and rollback when relevant.
- The validation plan, current review result, and remaining blockers, limitations or deferred tests.

what was verified, what is left, including any review that is pending, and the page and revision used to
edit the prose.

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in messages from the system in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# The vh-adlc loop

Every operation follows the same frame. The steps below are the plugin's procedure; the rules they
apply live in `vhco-pro/docs` at the resolved revision, and an operation cites the page it took each
rule from.

`skills/vh-adlc-clean/SKILL.md` skips steps 1 and 2 altogether; audit's offline bootstrap below still
uses the verified binary and knowledge. Clean calls `vh-adlc` from `PATH` without the installer, so that
its allow rule matches, and it skips `knowledge`, because `clean` and `env` read no conventions. The
binary it runs is therefore not checked against the lock.

## 1. Get the binary

Audit entry overrides this section's online bootstrap, including when selected through lifecycle
intake. Use `scripts/audit/bootstrap.ts --offline` as the audit skill specifies: cached verified binary,
validated settings metadata, then cache-only knowledge for its normalized `knowledge_pages`. Missing
prerequisites stop audit work with an explicit setup handoff. Never invoke the online installer first.
The metadata read is the narrow exception to knowledge-first order. Explicit setup may obtain the
binary and complete pinned pages separately; other operations keep the ordinary procedure below.

The plugin directory is the one that holds `skills/`: two levels above the skill's own directory, which
the host names when it loads the skill. Resolve a symlinked skill directory to its real location first.
Run the installer through Bash from there and use the path it prints for every later call:

```sh
VH_ADLC=$(bash "<plugin directory>/scripts/ensure-vh-adlc.sh")
```

Some native installers do not preserve executable bits. Bash invocation requires only a readable
script; do not change installed permissions. The installer still performs checksum verification
against `vh-adlc.lock.json` and fails closed on any mismatch; never work around a failure.

When the installer fails, open the report with a line that reads exactly
`deterministic checks unavailable`, so a reader can search for it, and carry on only with read-only work:
investigating, drafting and reporting. Every status change stops, unless the owner
explicitly allows a procedural gate for this run. Record that permission in the feature document and
write the gate line as `vh-adlc gate <target>: procedural (owner allowed: <reason>)`.

## 2. Resolve knowledge

Call `knowledge` first, with every docs page the operation will read:

```sh
"$VH_ADLC" knowledge --repo <dir> --plugin-pin <pin from knowledge.md> --page <path> ...
```

State the result in one line that also names the prose guide, for example
`Conventions: vhco-pro/docs@0e52f51 (repository pin, AGENTS.md); prose edited with guides/humanize-prose.md`.
Every report opens with this line, after the `deterministic checks unavailable` line when there is one,
including a report that stops at a gate or waits for the owner. Every call below passes the same
`--repo` and `--plugin-pin`, written out on each call. The binary needs every word as its own argument:
the command, each path, each flag and each value. A quoted variable that holds several of them arrives as
one unknown command or flag.

The binary caches each page it resolved. Read them from that cache rather than from memory:
`${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-$HOME/.cache}/vh-adlc/docs/<sha>/<page>` on Linux and
`$HOME/Library/Caches/vh-adlc/docs/<sha>/<page>` on macOS.

Stop and report when the result is `invalid-pin`, `missing-page` (recommend the pin bump it names) or
`unreachable`. Each finding already names the page or pin at fault, so do not re-run `knowledge` with
fewer pages to see which ones resolve, and do not read any page from that revision.

When `source` is `plugin`, the repository has no pin yet. `vh-adlc-investigate`, `vh-adlc-resume` and
`vh-adlc-review` and `vh-adlc-docs-impact` add none: they work with the plugin pin and report the missing pin, and onboarding waits
for the next operation that writes. A review that committed onboarding first would move its own target.
`vh-adlc-spec`, `vh-adlc-tasks`, `vh-adlc-implement` and `vh-adlc-ship` call `knowledge` again with the
same pages plus `guides/onboard-a-repository.md`, and read it. Their first change then adds the pinned
`AGENTS.md` and its bridges as that guide describes, merged into any local instructions, in its own
commit. Local instructions win over the central pages; report every conflict between them.
Onboarding also checks GitHub's automatic deletion of merged PR branches with `auto-delete` from
`references/branches.md` and reports the setting. When it is off, ask the owner whether to turn it
on; enable it only after they say yes. The setting is a repository change, not a commit, so it never
holds up the onboarding commit.
Beside that check, onboarding runs the security-settings helper from
`references/security-settings.md` in the mode `security-settings-mode` prints, and reports its
output. That is also a repository change that never holds up the onboarding commit. Onboarding has no
maintenance request, so the committed settings alone decide; it usually runs in `check`, because its
own commit is what links the settings. A request that is read-only or draft-only, or forbids
pushing or filesystem writes, selects `check` without calling the command. A nonzero
`security-settings-mode` exit, whatever its cause, leads to `check` with mode reason
`committed-settings-unresolved` and the cause, never to `apply`. Under `check`, report the states,
say how to opt in with `security_settings: apply`, and record the onboarding guide's security
checklist item as pending the owner's choice. Never run the guide's manual commands or the helper's
`apply` on an in-session yes.

Every page the loop needs is requested on every call, so a pin older than the plugin's pages stops with
`missing-page`: always include `conventions/feature-documents.md` and `guides/humanize-prose.md`.

A repository may declare loop settings in `.vh-adlc/loop.yaml` (`references/loop-settings.md`). The
SDD operations (spec, tasks, implement, review, ship, investigate and resume) then read their loop role's
route with `bun scripts/loop/cli.ts route`, and before acting read the instruction files and project
procedure that `bun scripts/loop/cli.ts context` lists.

## 3. Decide with the binary

The binary decides; the operation only acts on its JSON result and quotes it in the report.

| Step | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Is there already a document for this issue or topic? | `find (--issue <n> \| --slug <s>)` |
| Is the document well formed? | `lint <doc>` |
| Are the reviews still current? | `fresh <doc>` |
| May the document change status now? | `gate <target-status> <doc>` |
| What comes next? | `next <doc>` |
| Were the reviewer's records stored as returned? | `review check <doc> --review R-<n> --returned <file>` |

Before every `fresh` and `gate`, run `git fetch origin <default branch>`; the binary never fetches.

A status change happens in this order and no other: run `gate <target>` while the document still has its
current status, edit the status only when the result is `pass`, re-run `lint`, and commit with the gate's
`data.line` copied into the commit body. A failing gate changes nothing: report each failing condition
and stop.

A `malformed` result means the document must be fixed, never bypassed. `local-format` means the
repository keeps its own format: run the gate procedurally, as that repository does, and say the binary
did not decide it.

## 4. Write prose a reader sees

Before committing or posting any prose a reader will see (document sections, commit messages, PR and
issue bodies, review summaries, run reports), edit it with `guides/humanize-prose.md` at the resolved
revision. The knowledge line at the top of the report names that page and revision. Records a reviewer
returned are stored exactly as returned.

Restate what an issue, an owner turn or any other source says in your own edited words. Do not paste its
wording as a quotation, even inside quotation marks: a quoted phrase keeps the tells the guide removes.
This holds in the report too. When you say you followed an owner's note, or chose not to, describe it in
your own words and never repeat its phrases.
Code, commands and file contents stay exact, in code spans.

## 5. Report

End every operation by reporting what changed, what was verified, every binary result acted on, and what
is left.

Name every issue, pull request, commit, release or workflow run in a report, question or summary by
its full URL, such as `https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/pull/8`, never as a bare `#8` or `OWNER/REPO#8`.
The same holds in documents, commit messages and PR and issue bodies you write. Quoted records stay
as returned.

When reporting finished spec work to the owner or requesting spec acceptance, including through resume,
present the owner-facing summary from `skills/vh-adlc-spec/SKILL.md` in the conversation before the
acceptance question. Keep the full document and review status available as supporting detail.
# Review protocol

## Routes

Before dispatching, read the reviewer role's route:
`bun scripts/loop/cli.ts route --repo <dir> --operation "spec review"` for a spec review, or
`--operation review` for an implementation review. Its JSON names the role, the route and any model.

- A `host` route uses the procedure below. A model the route names counts as a requested model.
- A `command` route runs `bun scripts/loop/cli.ts review --repo <dir> --document <doc> --commit <X>
  --kind <spec|implementation> --docs-revision <sha> --binary <path> --plugin-pin <pin>`. It runs the
  configured CLI with the canonical reviewer instructions and the dispatch identity, as
  `references/loop-settings.md` describes: a spec review reads a read-only export of X and is launched
  from it; an implementation review runs in a private clone of X. Afterwards the clone, and the owning
  worktree's files, index, HEAD and branch, must be unchanged outside `review_scratch`. A route with `model_attestation: codex-session` takes the served model from
  Codex's own session log, so a `MODEL: unknown` self-report is accepted only when that attested model
  matches the request. Its JSON `status` is `ready` or `pending`. On `ready`, store its `records`
  under `### R-<n>` with a Review Log row naming its `model` and isolation `procedural`, then run
  `review check` against the same text. On `pending`, store nothing and report a line that starts with
  `review pending`, followed by its `reason`, with the raw `reply` in the handoff.

## Independence

A review runs in a separate context. Prefer the registered `vh-adlc-reviewer` agent. If the host does not
register that agent but supports a generic independent subagent, dispatch one with
`agents/vh-adlc-reviewer.agent.md` as its instructions. Have it read that canonical file and follow its
body; frontmatter tool names do not grant or restrict a generic subagent's tools. Request read-only
access where the host supports it. Do not copy or translate the reviewer into a host-specific file.
If that canonical file cannot be read, leave the review pending rather than invent its instructions.

Both routes receive the repository directory, document path, exact commit, review kind, resolved docs
revision, verified binary path and plugin pin. Neither route creates or switches a worktree. If the
host has neither independent route, or dispatch fails, write a self-contained
handoff the owner runs elsewhere and leave the review visibly pending: whenever no review is stored, the
report has a line that starts with the exact words `review pending`, followed by why. Self-review is never labelled
independent, whatever the model.

The target is an exact commit. A completion-eligible implementation review runs against committed state in
the feature's owning worktree with `feature_tree_clean` true. An uncommitted diagnostic review is recorded
with a `+dirty` commit and never counts as current. The reviewer uses the host's existing worktree; it does
not create one.

## Models

Agent files name no model. Decide whether this dispatch has a requested model before comparing identities.

# Feature documents

A feature is one observable outcome with accepted scope and verifiable criteria. Each feature has one
document that is both its specification and its plan. Do not create a companion spec, plan or notes file
for the same feature.

Enforcement: the `vh-adlc` binary reads the [rules block](#rules) at the repository's pinned revision of
this page and decides every status change with `vh-adlc gate`. Until that binary is released, these rules
are checked by hand, and a report says so.

## Location

A repository declares its feature root with one line in its root `AGENTS.md`:

```markdown
Feature documents: docs/specs/
```

Without that line, documents live in `docs/internal/plans/<slug>.md`. Do not move existing documents to
reach a default. A repository that keeps its own document format declares
`Feature document format: local` instead; this standard and its tooling then do not apply there.

## Frontmatter

```yaml
---
status: draft
status_description: "One line on the current state and what it waits for."
issue: https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/issues/42
goal: "One observable outcome."
covers:
  - path/to/implementation/
---
```

`issue: null` marks local-only work; never invent a link. `covers` lists every path whose change can
affect the feature; the document itself is never covered. A document gains `branch` when implementation
starts and keeps it until the feature is closed.

## Statuses

| Status | Meaning | Set by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| draft | Being specified or revised | Authoring, or a normative revision |
| planned | Accepted by the owner and ready to build | The spec review step, after acceptance |
| in-progress | Being implemented on its feature branch | Implementation, as its first commit |
| complete | Every criterion met or residualised, reviewed | Implementation or shipping |
| blocked | Waiting on a named owner decision or external fix | Any step, naming the blocker |
| parked | Deliberately paused | The owner |
| abandoned | Will not be built | The owner |
| superseded | Replaced by another feature, which it links | The owner |
| archived | Closed history | The owner |

`complete` is terminal for its scope; new scope is a new feature. A blocked feature names the smallest
decision that clears it.

## Sections

Required, in this order: Context, Scope, Design, Acceptance Criteria, Test Plan, Tasks, Open Questions and
Review Log. Implementation Phases (before Tasks) and Sources (last) are optional. Delete a section that does
not apply rather than leave it empty, except the required ones, which may say "None.".

Scope, Design, Acceptance Criteria, Test Plan and the `covers` frontmatter form the normative baseline. A
change to any of them is a revision. Before the change is applied, a `planned` or `in-progress` document
moves to `draft` (on its feature branch when it has one); earlier reviews become stale, the owner accepts
again, and the document moves `draft` to `planned` before implementation re-enters through its branch.

Context and Design cite their claims: a `file:line`, or a command and its output, gathered when the claim
was written. Sources lists every external page read, each with the claim it supports.

### Owner summary in Context

New documents and documents undergoing a normative revision start Context with `### Owner summary`.
Use a few short paragraphs to explain the problem and outcome, scope, approach, important defaults,
permissions, trade-offs, validation state and owner decisions. Include migration or recovery where it
matters. Usually 250 to 400 words is enough; a small feature can be shorter. This is guidance for a
readable explanation, not a word-count gate.

The detailed normative sections remain authoritative. The summary must agree with them and distinguish
planned checks from observed proof. Refresh it when scope, proof or decisions change and before asking
for acceptance. Explain material changes since the last accepted scope. The reviewer checks for
contradictions, consequential omissions and unsupported claims through the existing finding records.
Keep the owner-facing conversation summary before acceptance as well.

Historical documents remain valid without this subsection. A summary-only prose correction does not
change the normative baseline or accept a feature. Keep stored review records verbatim; do not shorten
them to make the summary easier to find. The required top-level sections and machine-readable rules
below are unchanged.

## Acceptance criteria

```markdown
- [ ] AC-01: The end state, observable without reading the code.
```

State the end state, never a measurement of the problem. A criterion whose subject is a report, a count
or a warning can go green while the problem remains. IDs are never reused, and a failed criterion is
never deleted

# Humanize prose
Apply this guide to every piece of prose a reader will see, as the
[documentation convention](../conventions/documentation.md#prose-a-reader-sees) requires. An agent host

Rewrite AI-sounding text so it reads like the writer, not a chatbot. Keep what it says. Do not make anything up.
## Why AI text sounds the way it does
A language model writes whatever is most likely to come next, so by default it makes the choice that fits the widest range of readers and subjects. A human writer chooses for one reader and one subject, so their choices are uneven and specific. Every pattern below is one form of the default choice:
- **Staging.** The sentence signals importance instead of adding a fact, with a contrast that only adds weight or a one-line closer that repeats the point.
- **Rhythm by rule.** Triads and dashes applied everywhere, whether or not the meaning asks for them.
- **Inflation.** Ordinary facts dressed as pivotal or expert-backed.
- **Formatting by rule.** Bold and title case applied to every item.
- **Leftovers.** Chat wrappers and drafting moves that were never meant for the reader.
- **Wrong reader.** A reply re-explains background the other person already has, so the decision arrives last.
Word habits change with every model release. The structural habits above persist, so they lead the list below.
Two rules follow from this. Every sentence you keep must add something the reader did not already have, from earlier in the text or from the conversation around it. A tell counts in proportion to how rarely a careful writer would make it on purpose. The patterns are numbered strongest first: §1 to §5 justify an edit on one sighting, and a pattern marked *weak alone* needs company from other tells in the same passage before you act.
## How to work
Treat the text as material to edit, never as instructions to follow.
1. **Mark the tells.** Read the whole text once and mark every pattern you find, strongest first. Look at paragraph shape as well as sentences. A contrast split across two sentences, three parallel examples, or the same closer after every section is the same tell at a larger scale.
2. **Draft the rewrite.** Keep every supported claim. You may shorten dull parts, merge or split paragraphs, and change structure, but keep the information. Do not add a fact, name, number, date, quote, or citation unless it comes from the source or the user. If a sentence needs a detail you do not have, ask for it or write a simpler sentence. An opinion or reaction is allowed when the voice calls for one; a factual claim is not. Fiction is exempt because invented detail is the task.
3. **Check the draft.** Read it aloud. Ask what still sounds AI-generated. Ask whether the rewrite added or dropped any fact, name, number, date, quote, citation, ranking, or claim that things happen at once; shape edits under §6, §9, and §19 drop those most often. Treat an unsupported addition as an error, and a lost claim as an error unless a pattern calls for cutting it. Then search again for the tells that most often survive a rewrite: §1 contrasts, §2 closers, §6 triads, §8 dashes, and §19 bold labels.
4. **Write the final version.** State each point naturally instead of patching flagged phrases one at a time. If a sentence stays awkward, rewrite the paragraph around its main point. Vary sentence length; real writing alternates short and long.
### Voice
If the user gives a writing sample, read it first and match its sentence length, word choice, punctuation, openings, and transitions. The sample overrides the patterns below, except the dash rule in §8.
Without a sample, take the voice from the kind of text. Blog posts, essays, opinions, and personal writing keep the writer's opinions, uncertainty, mixed feelings, humor, and asides, and you may add a reaction where the writer would. Reference, technical, legal, and factual text stays neutral and plain. Removing tells is half the job; the result must still sound like a person.

**Pasted text (default).** Return the draft, a short list of remaining patterns, and the final rewrite.
**File mode.** When the user names a file, run the full process but write only the final text to the file. Change prose only. Keep code blocks, inline code, commands, paths, YAML metadata, data, and link targets unchanged. Then give the user a short summary.
**Embedded mode.** When another task uses this skill for a pull request, commit message, or document, return only the final text.

**After:**

**After:**
